newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tajik opposition suspends Tehran peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Tajik opposition suspends Tehran peace talks.

text.p: Tajikistan's Islamic opposition halted peace talks with the former Soviet republic's government almost as soon as they began in Tehran on Wednesday, Russia's Itar-Tass news agency reported from the Iranian capital.

It quoted deputy opposition leader Akbar Turadjonzoda as telling journalists he was suspending negotiations for several days over what he alleged was the arrest of 11 opposition members in Moscow on charges of "terrorism".
Tajik Foreign Minister Talbak Nazarov, leading the delegation from the pro-Moscow government in Dushanbe, was quoted as saying he knew nothing of the alleged arrests.
Russian officials could not be reached for comment.
The negotiations, the latest in a series over recent months that has already produced a ceasefire in the Central Asian state's four-year civil war, began only on Wednesday morning.
The United Nations special envoy to Tajikistan Gerd Merrem was also in Tehran for the talks, the Iranian news agency IRNA said.
The talks are to focus on ways of legalising opposition organisations, officials from both sides have said.
Observers from Iran, Russia, Pakistan and Uzbekistan were attending the negotiations, which were expected to last 10 days, IRNA said just after the meeting got under way.
A military deal was agreed last month in Moscow between the main protagonists in the civil war. A four-month-old ceasefire appears to be holding.

In February, the government and the opposition hailed a preliminary power-sharing agreement reached after talks in Iran which gave each side an equal number of seats on a 26-member National Commission for Reconciliation.

The commission was limited to members of the government and the Islamic opposition. Diplomats fear the commission could sideline other groups, although legalisation of opposition political parties would give them a greater voice.
Tens of thousands lost their lives in the bloody civil war and many more were made homeless in the remote mountainous republic of 5.7 million people.
